title: Automatic and Universal Prompt Injection Attacks against Large Language Models
evaluated: Seven NLP user tasks (MRPC duplicate sentence detection, Jfleg grammar correction, hate content detection, NLI, sentiment analysis, spam detection, Gigaword summarization) on victim Llama2-7b-chat; three attack objectives (static, semi-dynamic, dynamic); baselines: combined prompt injection attack (Liu et al.), repeated characters attack, naive attack; defenses: paraphrasing, retokenization, external data isolation, instructional prevention, sandwich prevention; ablation GCG vs M-GCG; metrics keyword ASR and LLM-evaluation ASR
quote: We introduce an automatic prompt injection attack method demonstrating strong universality across various user interactions and datasets. (Section 1, Introduction - contributions list)
notes: The attack itself is unnamed (matching current_registry_entry 'UNNAMED'); the only proper names the paper coins are M-GCG (its optimizer) and the three attack-objective categories (static / semi-dynamic / dynamic objective), which are objective taxonomies rather than attack names. Later work cites this as 'Universal Prompt Injection' from the repo name, not from a name the paper assigns. Hence names_registry_technique=unsure rather than a confident no. Note also a scope gap: the title and abstract claim 'universal' attacks against LLMs generally, but the evaluation uses a single victim model (Llama2-7b-chat), so universality is demonstrated across tasks/instructions, not across models.

title: Dynamic Parametric Retrieval Augmented Generation for Test-time Knowledge Enhancement
evaluated: F1 on 2WikiMultihopQA, HotpotQA, PopQA and ComplexWebQuestions with Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, LLaMA-3.2-1B-Instruct, LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct; baselines Vanilla, Standard RAG, PRAG, PRAG-Combine; inference/training/storage cost comparison; RAGTruth benchmark with GPT-4o as judge comparing standard RAG vs DyPRAG-Combine; appendix analysis of contextual-vs-parametric knowledge conflict
quote: To address these challenges, we propose Dynamic Parametric RAG (DyPRAG), a novel framework that leverages a lightweight parameter translator model to efficiently convert documents into parametric knowledge. (Abstract)
notes: CLAIM/EVALUATION MISMATCH. The abstract claims DyPRAG resolves knowledge conflicts and mitigates RAG hallucination, but the main evaluation is F1 accuracy on four QA datasets (2WikiMultihopQA, HotpotQA, PopQA, CWQ) plus inference/training/storage cost; the knowledge-conflict and hallucination claims rest on a secondary RAGTruth comparison judged by GPT-4o and on qualitative appendix case studies, with no measured conflict rate or hallucination rate reduction. Explicitly an extension of PRAG, so improves_existing, not the registry's 'proposed'. belongs_in_corpus marked unsure because the paper's core concern is RAG cost/efficiency and parametric knowledge injection rather than context becoming untrustworthy; the knowledge-conflict framing is what keeps it borderline in scope.

title: Adversarial Attacks of Vision Tasks in the Past 10 Years: A Survey
quote: This article addresses these gaps by offering a thorough summary of traditional and LVLM adversarial attacks, emphasizing their connections and distinctions, and providing actionable insights for future research. (Abstract)
notes: Ten-year survey of visual adversarial attacks. No experiments of its own, hence 'no evaluation'. It catalogues and taxonomises pre-existing named attacks (adversarial examples, data/model poisoning, backdoor, and for LVLMs: cognitive bias, prompt injection, jailbreak, typography, conditional image generation) but coins no attack or failure-mode name of its own, so names_registry_technique=no. belongs_in_corpus marked 'unsure' on scope grounds rather than contribution grounds: the bulk of the survey is pixel-space evasion attacks on vision classifiers, which is adversarial input but not untrustworthy *context* in the agent sense; only Section 7 (LVLM attacks: prompt injection, typographic/CIG attacks on image content the model reads) is on-topic. Registry had no entry.

title: Anatomy of Agentic Memory: Taxonomy and Empirical Analysis of Evaluation and System Limitations
evaluated: Six memory-augmented systems (A-MEM, MemoryOS, Nemori, MAGMA, SimpleMem, MemSkill) with gpt-4o-mini and Qwen-2.5-3B controllers over HotpotQA, LoCoMo, LongMemEval-S/M and MemBench; structural saturation-risk analysis of those benchmarks; lexical F1 vs LLM-judge disagreement cases; latency/throughput overhead
quote: This survey presents a structured analysis of agentic memory from both architectural and system perspectives. (Abstract)
notes: Survey plus original measurements; it introduces a diagnostic metric, the Context Saturation Gap, and failure labels for lexical metrics (Surface Variation, Semantic Equivalence Gap, Polarity Flip, Entity Drift), but these are evaluation-methodology artefacts, not agent failure modes other papers test against, so names_registry_technique=no. No claim/evaluation mismatch marker: the paper measures what it claims (benchmark saturation, metric validity, backbone sensitivity, latency). Scope is genuinely uncertain: nothing in it concerns untrustworthy or attacker-controlled content; the subject is memory-system capability, cost and evaluation validity, touching context saturation and lost-in-the-middle only as regimes where memory helps. Marked unsure rather than no because it is a survey of context/memory management rather than a capability benchmark. Registry had no entry.

title: RAG-Modulo: Solving Sequential Tasks using Experience, Critics, and Language Models
evaluated: BabyAI-Synth, BabyAI-BossLevel, AlfWorld-Seen (140 instances) and AlfWorld-Unseen (132 instances); baselines Expert, ProgPrompt and LLM-Planner; metrics success rate (SR), infeasible executions (InExec) and plan length (Len), with GPT-4o as the planner and text-embedding-3-large as retriever; ablations over number of retrieved interactions K and over retrieval granularity (interaction-level vs skill-level).
quote: We propose RAG-Modulo, a framework that enhances LLM-based agents with a memory of past interactions and incorporates critics to evaluate the agents’ decisions. (Abstract)
notes: Borderline scope, kept in the corpus but flagged. The paper's stated problem is a capability gap (LLM agents cannot learn from past interactions in long-horizon robotic tasks), not untrustworthy context, and the headline metrics are task success rate, infeasible-execution count and plan length on BabyAI and AlfWorld. What keeps it arguably relevant is one ablation: varying the number K of retrieved past interactions produces a rise-then-fall curve, which the authors attribute to the model's sensitivity to irrelevant or noisy retrieved context (citing Shi et al. on distraction by irrelevant context and Liu et al. 'Lost in the Middle'), concluding that K between 5 and 10 is best. That is a distractor-density ablation measuring retrieval-noise degradation directly, so no CLAIM/EVALUATION MISMATCH marker -- the paper never claims to solve a context problem in the first place. Registry entry 'defense: RAG-Modulo' is wrong on genre: there is no adversary; it is an extension of LLM-Modulo with episodic memory and critics, hence improves_existing.

title: Still: Amortized KV Cache Compaction in a Single Forward Pass
evaluated: RULER long-context grid (contexts 8k-128k, compression ratios 8x-200x) on Qwen and Gemma; HELMET free-form summarization; pairwise LongBench summarization comparison against KV-Distill; held-out multidomain MCQ accuracy (Legal, Financial, Gutenberg, Code) at fixed compression and across context lengths up to 64k/128k; baselines = KV-Distill, per-context selection methods, Cartridges, Attention Matching, full-context and no-context references; metrics accuracy, KL/CE proxy losses, utilization, speed-quality frontier
quote: On the long-context RULER grid, Still exceeds the strongest baseline by 8–22 points. (Abstract)
notes: No mismatch marker: the paper does NOT frame itself around a context failure mode at all (no context rot, dilution, distraction or lost-in-the-middle claim), so Ruling 1 does not trigger. It is a systems paper about the KV cache as a memory bottleneck, and it measures exactly what it claims - fidelity retained under compaction (RULER, HELMET, LongBench summarization, held-out MCQ accuracy as a function of compression ratio and context length) plus speed. Scope is genuinely borderline, hence belongs_in_corpus = unsure: 'context' is used in the correct literal sense and information loss under compaction is a non-adversarial context-degradation failure, but there is no untrustworthy content and no adversary anywhere, and the motivation is purely memory and serving cost. Note this is the same genre as row 47 (LCLM); whichever way the lead decides, rows 47 and 60 should be treated the same. Registry disagreement: 'defense: Still (amortized KV cache compaction, Perceiver)' is wrong in kind - no adversary, so not a defense. FIX-NAME: Still (per-layer Perceiver compactor producing compact keys and values in a single forward pass; iterative compaction).

title: Multi-Agent Firewall Architecture for Privacy Protection of Sensitive Data in Interactions with Language Models
evaluated: nvidia/Nemotron-PII test split (us locale, 500 cases, fixed seed), run as an 11-configuration ablation (deterministic regex only, GLiNER NER threshold sweep 0.3/0.5/0.7/0.85, forced-LLM exhaustive detection with gemma-3-4b-it, Ministral-3-8B, Llama-3.1-8B, gemma-4-E4B); metrics are precision, recall, F1 (up to 94.93%) and latency. No attack suite, no prompt-injection evaluation.
quote: This paper proposes an open-source, privacy-focused, user-facing firewall designed to secure both web-based and programmatic LLM interactions. (Abstract)
notes: DEFENSE-NAMES: (unnamed; the artifact is only referred to by its package name 'multiagent-firewall'). SCOPE CONCERN: the threat direction is outbound, not inbound - this is a data-leakage-prevention firewall stopping users from sending PII and proprietary code INTO an LLM, not an agent reading context it should not trust. Prompt-injection evasion is listed only as a future extensible component and is explicitly excluded from the evaluation (Sec. 5.1 also excludes multimodal analysis, code-similarity detection and anonymization fidelity). So it is a real, implemented, evaluated defense, but arguably against a different problem than context poisoning - hence belongs_in_corpus=unsure rather than a flat no. Registry entry 'defense: UNNAMED: multi-agent privacy firewall (browser...)' is accurate as far as it goes. No CLAIM/EVALUATION MISMATCH marker: the paper claims PII/leakage detection and measures PII/leakage detection.
